--- Page 8 --- REPORT ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF TIE COSSYAH AND JYNTEAH HILL TERRITORY.
FROM W.
ALLEN, ESQUIRE, Meniber of the Bourd of Rerenue, on Vepuiation, To A.
YOUNG, ESQUIRE.
Secrctary to the Government of Bengal, FORT WILIIAM.
Dated Cherru Poonjce, the 1lth Octaber 1853.
SIR, I Have the honor to report the result of the inquiries which I have made with refercnce to the Orders of Government, No.
116, of the I9th of January 1$57, into thc existing method of administering the Civil, Criminal, Ruvenue, and General Affairs of the Cossyah and Jynteah Hill Territory.

Mills visited Cherra Poonjee in August I853, and iis Report on that district contains a full and conplete represcntation of thc state of affairs in these Hills at that period ; it scems necessary, thercfore, to notice now only what nay have oceurred since then, to explain what measures havc been adopt- ed subseQuent to 1853 for the improvemcnt of the administration of publie afairs, and to show what has been the practical cffect of those neasures.
The Civil functions of the Political Agent in the Cossyah ills, and the Command of the Sylhet Light Infantry Battalion, which had been conjointly beld by Lieutenant-Colonel Lister since Feb- *No.525.
ruary 1835, were separated from each other by Orders* of the Most Noble the Governor ot Bengal, dated the 1ith of March 1854.

and the General, Civil and Political Administration of the Cossyan and Jynteah Hill Ferritory was transferred to an Assistant attached to the Assam Commission, who was placed " preciscly on thc same footing as the " other Principal Assistants in the Province of A ssam." 4.

Hudson, Junior Assistant Commissioner, was deputed by the Commissioner to Cherra Poonjec, as an Oficiating Principal Assistant Com- : - inissioner, and took charge of the district on the 10th of April 1854, from Lieu- : tenant G.
Cave, who was officiating as Political Agent during theabsence :.
of Lieutenant-Colonel Lister, who had proceeded to England on sick loave.
It appears that the Commissioner of Assam gavo no instructions whatever to Mr.
Hudson, in regard to the nanner in which his duties were to be conducted ; but being an Oficer of the Assan Commission, Mr.
Hudson very naturally and properly considered himself bound, in his of- cial proceedings, to follow, as much as possible, the rules, orders and prac- tice of the Assan Courts.

No Public Notifieation, howover, has been pub- lished, cither by the Government or the Local Anthorities, regarding the transfer of this district to the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of Assam, and the public las never been officially informed what laws, rulos and regulations are in forco in this Hill Territory.

Bofore proceeding to make any general remarks upon the state of affairs in these Hill-, I purpose to notice the allegations and accusations con- tained in the Memorials and Correspondence referred to in the 2nd para.
of the Government Orders, and shall endeavour to show what the facts reully are which have been represented in such different lights by the contending parties.
Messrs.
Coleman, Haddan and Brownlow, and certain Caleutta Merchants, wish to make out, that Mr.
Inglis is a lawless oppressor and a momopolist, who upholds and carries on his nefarious comnercial speculations by fraud and violence, whilst Mr.

Inglis stigmatizes his opponents and accusers as a noisy knot of unprincipled and reekless adventurers, who are endeavouring to encroach upon and ruin lis long-established and legitimate trade in these Hills, by tampering with the Hill people, with whom hc has commcrcial dealings, and by cxciting then b: false and delusive promises to repudiate their lawful engagemnents with him.

When I arrived at Cherra Poonjee at the cnd of March 1s57, I sent, from the Ofices of the Principal Assistant Commissioncr at Cherra Poonjee and the Magistrate of Sylhet, for all the cascs in which Mr.
Inglis and his opponents had been concerned, and soon afterwards Messrs.
Coleman, Had- dan, Halford Brownlow an other Gentlemen came to Cherra Poonjee to make known their grievances personally to me.
I have receivcd fron the Sylhot Magistrate 21 cases, and from the Cherra Court 36 cascs, nall of which I have very attentively cxamined and con-idered.
The gravest of the charges and complaints made against Mr, H.
Inglis and the persons sup- posed to bc his dopendents and partisans, are those of Messrs.
Coleman, Haddan and Brownlow.
I shall, therefore, proceed to report upon them first.
I found that.

although the offenccs charged by these three Gentle- men had been comnmitted in the Cherra jurisdiction, no legal progeedings had boen taken by them in the Cherra Court : complaints had been made to the Magistrate of Sylhet, and certain inquiries had been instituted into them by that Oficer, but no final orders had been passed.
It.appears that.
when these cases were first reported, both the Principal Assistant Cornmis- sioner and the Sylhet Magistrate entertained doubts as to whether.

the place where tho offences had been committed, was in the Sylhet or the --- Page 10 --- (3) Hill district; this question might have bcen casily and immediately scttled by eithecr of the district Officers, bnt no decision thereon was given by either of them for more than fivc months.
From inquirics which I have made there can be no doubt, in my opinion, that thc Cherra, Court had jurisdiction in these cases.
When I asked Messrs.

Coleman, Haddan and Halford Brownlow, why thcy had not prosecuted thcir charges in the usual mauner in the Cherrat Court, they replied that they felt no confidenee in that Court, becausc it was under the infuence or Mr.
Inglis, and they moreover stated that they did not dare to enter the Hill Territory again till they werc guarantecd personal .protection against Mr.
Inglis and his servants.

1 pointed out to thcm, that it was not too latc to proceed with their cases in the Chcrra Court ; but they declined dring so, and stated that the inquiries nade by the Magistrate of Sylhet clearly proved their charges, and that they were willing to rest their cases on thosc proceedings.
They added that their witnesses wcre not then at hand, and that they could not afford the expense and trouble of another prosecution.
They furthernore reprc sented, that thcir present objeet was not.

so much to procure the punish- ment of the offenders, as to demonstrate and prove to the Govermment how who sought to establish commcrcial intercourse with these Hill people, owing to the baneful infuence and illegal and violent proccedings of Mr.
llenry Inglis.
Wuen the matter tcok this turn, I forwarded all the papers of thesc cases to the Principal Assistant Commissioner, and instructed him to allow Mr.
Inglis and all the otier parties accused, to inspect tho records, and to submit any defence or explanation they might desire to ofler in regard to the statements that had been matde against them.
I also directed the Principal Assistant Commnissioner to take any evidence that they might be able to bring forward to rebut these grave charges.
These orders have been carefully carried out by the Principnl Assistant Commissioncr, and the cases arc now complete enough to enable me to form an opinion in regard to their merits.
The facts of Mr.
Coleman's case, as they appeared in evidence, are as follows.

He arrived at Kuppreya Bazaar, in the Cheyla district, on Wednesday, the Sth of October .1856, and took up .
